claim: Climate warming is releasing carbon from soils around the world, constituting a positive climate feedback.
source: Climate warming is releasing carbon from soils around the world, constituting a positive climate feedback.
evidence: Supported by citation to Canadell et al., 2021

claim: Warming is causing species to expand their ranges into new ecosystems.
source: Warming is also causing species to expand their ranges into new ecosystems.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on range expansions

claim: Warming led to a negligible decrease in alpine soil carbon content.
source: We found that warming (transplantation to low elevation) led to a negligible decrease in alpine soil carbon content, but its effects became significant and 52% ± 31% (mean ± 95% confidence intervals) larger after lowland plants were introduced at low density into the ecosystem.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from two field transplant experiments

claim: The effects of warming on alpine soil carbon content became significant and 52% ± 31% larger after lowland plants were introduced at low density.
source: We found that warming (transplantation to low elevation) led to a negligible decrease in alpine soil carbon content, but its effects became significant and 52% ± 31% (mean ± 95% confidence intervals) larger after lowland plants were introduced at low density into the ecosystem.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from two field transplant experiments with statistical analysis

claim: Decreases in soil carbon content likely occurred via lowland plants increasing rates of root exudation, soil microbial respiration, and CO2 release under warming.
source: We present evidence that decreases in soil carbon content likely occurred via lowland plants increasing rates of root exudation, soil microbial respiration, and CO2 release under warming.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from glasshouse and field experiments showing increased microbial respiration and DOM changes

claim: Warming-induced range expansions of herbaceous plants have the potential to alter climate feedbacks from alpine ecosystems.
source: Our findings suggest that warming-induced range expansions of herbaceous plants have the potential to alter climate feedbacks from this system, and that plant range expansions among herbaceous communities may be an overlooked mediator of warming effects on carbon dynamics.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results showing lowland plant effects on soil carbon

claim: Plant range expansions among herbaceous communities may be an overlooked mediator of warming effects on carbon dynamics.
source: Our findings suggest that warming-induced range expansions of herbaceous plants have the potential to alter climate feedbacks from this system, and that plant range expansions among herbaceous communities may be an overlooked mediator of warming effects on carbon dynamics.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and gap in existing literature

claim: Climate warming is expected to accelerate the release of soil carbon to the atmosphere.
source: Climate warming is expected to accelerate the release of soil carbon to the atmosphere (Canadell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Canadell et al., 2021

claim: Warming is driving uphill and poleward range expansions of native plant species around the globe.
source: At the same time, warming is driving uphill and poleward range expansions of native plant species around the globe (Parmesan, 2006; Lenoir and Svenning, 2015; Pecl et al., 2017; Dolezal et al., 2016; Rumpf et al., 2018; Steinbauer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting range expansions

claim: The impact of range expanding plants on soil carbon storage under warming remains poorly understood.
source: Yet while warming and plant range expansions are now co-occurring in many terrestrial ecosystems, the impact of range expanding plants on soil carbon storage under warming remains poorly understood (Wallingford et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation and represents a knowledge gap

claim: Plant species adapted to different temperatures can have contrasting effects on carbon cycle processes.
source: This is important because plant species adapted to different temperatures can have contrasting effects on carbon cycle processes (Walker et al., 2019), raising the potential for migrating species to have qualitatively different impacts on carbon dynamics from resident plants.
evidence: Supported by citation to Walker et al., 2019

claim: The arrival of novel species in a community can alter carbon cycling in recipient ecosystems.
source: For example, studies of non-native species invasions have revealed that the arrival of novel species in a community can alter carbon cycling in recipient ecosystems (Liao et al., 2008; Waller et al., 2020), while woody plant expansions into treeless Arctic ecosystems can reverse the direction of carbon cycle feedbacks to climate warming (Pearson et al., 2013; Cornelissen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on non-native species invasions

claim: Woody plant expansions into treeless Arctic ecosystems can reverse the direction of carbon cycle feedbacks to climate warming.
source: For example, studies of non-native species invasions have revealed that the arrival of novel species in a community can alter carbon cycling in recipient ecosystems (Liao et al., 2008; Waller et al., 2020), while woody plant expansions into treeless Arctic ecosystems can reverse the direction of carbon cycle feedbacks to climate warming (Pearson et al., 2013; Cornelissen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pearson et al., 2013 and Cornelissen et al., 2007

claim: The majority of warming-induced range expansions occur among native communities of similar species.
source: However, the majority of warming-induced range expansions do not involve non-native species or novel growth forms, but occur among native communities of similar species (e.g. Steinbauer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steinbauer et al., 2018

claim: We know remarkably little about how migrations of herbaceous plants into predominantly herbaceous ecosystems will affect carbon cycling.
source: In particular, we know remarkably little about how migrations of herbaceous plants into predominantly herbaceous ecosystems will affect carbon cycling, and so the magnitude and direction of resulting climate feedbacks are unknown.
evidence: Represents a knowledge gap in the literature

claim: Alpine ecosystems occur in the uppermost elevations of the planet as cool islands within warmer landscapes that are bounded by steep gradients in temperature.
source: Alpine ecosystems occur in the uppermost elevations of the planet as cool islands within warmer landscapes that are bounded by steep gradients in temperature (Körner, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Körner, 2003

claim: Alpine ecosystems are experiencing rapid temperature change (0.4–0.6°C per decade).
source: They are experiencing both rapid temperature change (0.4–0.6°C per decade) (Pepin, 2015; Vitasse et al., 2021) and rapid species immigration (Lenoir et al., 2008), the latter of which involves an influx of herbaceous warm-adapted species from lowlands into herbaceous cold-adapted communities at higher elevations (Dolezal et al., 2016; Rumpf et al., 2018; Steinbauer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pepin, 2015 and Vitasse et al., 2021

claim: Alpine ecosystems are experiencing rapid species immigration.
source: They are experiencing both rapid temperature change (0.4–0.6°C per decade) (Pepin, 2015; Vitasse et al., 2021) and rapid species immigration (Lenoir et al., 2008), the latter of which involves an influx of herbaceous warm-adapted species from lowlands into herbaceous cold-adapted communities at higher elevations (Dolezal et al., 2016; Rumpf et al., 2018; Steinbauer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Alpine species immigration involves an influx of herbaceous warm-adapted species from lowlands into herbaceous cold-adapted communities at higher elevations.
source: They are experiencing both rapid temperature change (0.4–0.6°C per decade) (Pepin, 2015; Vitasse et al., 2021) and rapid species immigration (Lenoir et al., 2008), the latter of which involves an influx of herbaceous warm-adapted species from lowlands into herbaceous cold-adapted communities at higher elevations (Dolezal et al., 2016; Rumpf et al., 2018; Steinbauer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dolezal et al., 2016; Rumpf et al., 2018; Steinbauer et al., 2018

claim: Alpine ecosystems hold more than 90% of their total ecosystem carbon in the soil.
source: Coupled to this, alpine ecosystems are globally relevant reservoirs of soil carbon and hold more than 90% of their total ecosystem carbon in the soil (Streit et al., 2014; Parker et al., 2015; Knowles et al., 2019; Hagedorn et al., 2019; Budge et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Alpine ecosystems are globally relevant reservoirs of soil carbon.
source: Coupled to this, alpine ecosystems are globally relevant reservoirs of soil carbon and hold more than 90% of their total ecosystem carbon in the soil (Streit et al., 2014; Parker et al., 2015; Knowles et al., 2019; Hagedorn et al., 2019; Budge et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Transplantation from high to low elevation caused a small decline in alpine soil carbon content in both regions.
source: We found that transplantation from high to low elevation (i.e. warming-only) caused a small decline in alpine soil carbon content, but in both regions this effect was stronger and only became statistically significant when lowland plants were also planted-in (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1; p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and statistical analysis

claim: The addition of lowland plants to transplanted alpine turfs increased warming-induced soil carbon loss from 4.1 ± 0.23 mg g−1 per °C to 6.3 mg g−1 per °C.
source: Specifically, considering field data from both experiments together, the addition of lowland plants to transplanted alpine turfs increased warming-induced soil carbon loss from 4.1 ± 0.23 mg g−1 per °C to 6.3 mg g−1 per °C, which is a 52% ± 31% (mean ± 95% confidence intervals [CIs]) increase relative to warming alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; p = 0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Uphill migrations of lowland plants are already globally common.
source: We thus suggest that uphill migrations of lowland plants, which are already globally common (Rumpf et al., 2018; Lenoir et al., 2008), may have a hitherto unrecognized bearing over alpine soil carbon storage.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rumpf et al., 2018 and Lenoir et al., 2008

claim: Soil carbon loss occurs due to a shifting balance between soil carbon inputs via net primary production and soil carbon outputs via soil microbial respiration.
source: Soil carbon loss occurs due to a shifting balance between soil carbon inputs via net primary production and soil carbon outputs via soil microbial respiration (Allison et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to established understanding of soil carbon dynamics

claim: Lowland plant treatments produced more aboveground biomass than alpine plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: We found that lowland plant treatments produced more aboveground (Figure 2a; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.028) and belowground (Figure 2b; Supplementary file 2; p < 0.001) biomass than alpine plants, while also containing a higher proportion of root tissue (root-to-shoot ratio: Figure 2c; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a with statistical analysis

claim: Lowland plant treatments produced more belowground biomass than alpine plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: We found that lowland plant treatments produced more aboveground (Figure 2a; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.028) and belowground (Figure 2b; Supplementary file 2; p < 0.001) biomass than alpine plants, while also containing a higher proportion of root tissue (root-to-shoot ratio: Figure 2c; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b with statistical analysis

claim: Lowland plant treatments contained a higher proportion of root tissue than alpine plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: We found that lowland plant treatments produced more aboveground (Figure 2a; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.028) and belowground (Figure 2b; Supplementary file 2; p < 0.001) biomass than alpine plants, while also containing a higher proportion of root tissue (root-to-shoot ratio: Figure 2c; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c with statistical analysis

claim: Lowland plant treatments possessed similar specific leaf area (SLA) to alpine plant treatments in the glasshouse experiment.
source: This occurred despite lowland plant treatments possessing similar specific leaf area (SLA: Figure 2d; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.861) to alpine plant treatments, as well as lower maximal photosynthetic capacity (Amax: Figure 2e; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.026) and stomatal conductance (gs: Figure 2f; Supplementary file 2; p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d with statistical analysis

claim: Lowland plant treatments had lower maximal photosynthetic capacity than alpine plant treatments in the glasshouse experiment.
source: This occurred despite lowland plant treatments possessing similar specific leaf area (SLA: Figure 2d; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.861) to alpine plant treatments, as well as lower maximal photosynthetic capacity (Amax: Figure 2e; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.026) and stomatal conductance (gs: Figure 2f; Supplementary file 2; p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e with statistical analysis

claim: Lowland plant treatments had lower stomatal conductance than alpine plant treatments in the glasshouse experiment.
source: This occurred despite lowland plant treatments possessing similar specific leaf area (SLA: Figure 2d; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.861) to alpine plant treatments, as well as lower maximal photosynthetic capacity (Amax: Figure 2e; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.026) and stomatal conductance (gs: Figure 2f; Supplementary file 2; p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f with statistical analysis

claim: Lower photosynthetic capacity and stomatal conductance in lowland plants suggests that photosynthetic capacity was limited by stomata pore size rather than by photosynthetic machinery.
source: While the reason for decreased photosynthetic capacity and stomatal conductance in the lowland plant treatment is unclear, the fact that both variables were lower suggests that photosynthetic capacity was limited by stomata pore size rather than by photosynthetic machinery (Wong et al., 1979).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and citation to Wong et al., 1979

claim: Lowland plants accelerated soil microbial respiration relative to alpine plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: We found that lowland plants accelerated soil microbial respiration relative to alpine plants (Figure 3a; treatment × time: likelihood ratio [LR] = 147.99, p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a with statistical analysis

claim: Soil under lowland plants contained more dissolved organic matter (DOM) than soil under alpine plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: Accelerated microbial activity was also reflected in spectral analyses of soil pore water, which showed that soil under lowland plants contained more dissolved organic matter (DOM) (Figure 4a, b; Supplementary file 2; absorbance [a350]: p < 0.001, total fluorescence [Ftot]: p < 0.001) with a higher proportion of microbially derived products (Figure 4c; Supplementary file 2; fluorescence index [FI]; p = 0.002) than soil under alpine plants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a, b with statistical analysis

claim: Soil under lowland plants had a higher proportion of microbially derived DOM products than soil under alpine plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: Accelerated microbial activity was also reflected in spectral analyses of soil pore water, which showed that soil under lowland plants contained more dissolved organic matter (DOM) (Figure 4a, b; Supplementary file 2; absorbance [a350]: p < 0.001, total fluorescence [Ftot]: p < 0.001) with a higher proportion of microbially derived products (Figure 4c; Supplementary file 2; fluorescence index [FI]; p = 0.002) than soil under alpine plants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c with statistical analysis

claim: Microbial respiration was enhanced despite no changes to microbial biomass between lowland and alpine plant treatments in the glasshouse experiment.
source: Importantly, microbial respiration was enhanced despite no changes to microbial biomass between treatments (Figure 3d; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.693), showing that microbes respired intrinsically faster (i.e. per unit of biomass) in the presence of lowland plants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d with statistical analysis

claim: Microbes respired intrinsically faster (per unit of biomass) in the presence of lowland plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: Importantly, microbial respiration was enhanced despite no changes to microbial biomass between treatments (Figure 3d; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.693), showing that microbes respired intrinsically faster (i.e. per unit of biomass) in the presence of lowland plants.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing enhanced respiration without biomass changes

claim: Soils supporting any plant contained a soil carbon pool that was effectively absent from a bare soil control in the glasshouse experiment.
source: First, two-pool models of microbial respiration revealed that soils supporting any plant contained a soil carbon pool that was effectively absent from a bare soil control, and which was a factor of 1.5 ± 0.7 (mean ± standard error [SE]) times larger under lowland plants than alpine plants (Figure 3b; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.046).
evidence: Supported by two-pool modeling of experimental data shown in Figure 3b

claim: The plant-associated soil carbon pool was 1.5 ± 0.7 times larger under lowland plants than alpine plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: First, two-pool models of microbial respiration revealed that soils supporting any plant contained a soil carbon pool that was effectively absent from a bare soil control, and which was a factor of 1.5 ± 0.7 (mean ± standard error [SE]) times larger under lowland plants than alpine plants (Figure 3b; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.046).
evidence: Supported by two-pool modeling of experimental data shown in Figure 3b with statistical analysis

claim: The plant-associated carbon pool decayed at a similar rate between lowland and alpine plant treatments in the glasshouse experiment.
source: This carbon pool decayed at a similar rate between treatments (Figure 3c; Supplementary file 2; p = 0.631), indicating that it differed in size, but likely not composition, between lowland and alpine treatments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c with statistical analysis

claim: The plant-associated carbon pool had a half-life of 5.1 ± 0.4 days in the glasshouse experiment.
source: Second, the same carbon pool was consumed rapidly by soil microbes (half-life = 5.1 ± 0.4 days), and we also found that lowland plant effects on microbial respiration were lost after 9 days of incubation without plants (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and two-pool modeling

claim: Lowland plant effects on microbial respiration were lost after 9 days of incubation without plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: Second, the same carbon pool was consumed rapidly by soil microbes (half-life = 5.1 ± 0.4 days), and we also found that lowland plant effects on microbial respiration were lost after 9 days of incubation without plants (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: A 9-day decay period corresponds to the time expected for newly photosynthesized carbon dioxide to be released through root exudation and respired by soil microbes.
source: While not directly measured here, a 9-day decay period corresponds to the time expected for newly photosynthesized carbon dioxide to be released through root exudation and respired by soil microbes (Hafner et al., 2012; Studer et al., 2014), suggesting that this carbon pool was mostly root exudates.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hafner et al., 2012 and Studer et al., 2014

claim: DOM contained a higher relative abundance of protein-like substances than humic-like and fulvic acid-like substances under lowland plants than alpine plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: Finally, DOM contained a higher relative abundance of protein-like substances than humic-like and fulvic acid-like substances (Figure 4d–i; Supplementary file 2; p < 0.01 in all cases) under lowland plants than alpine plants, also suggesting that lowland plants caused an enrichment in exudate-derived compounds (Jones et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d-i with statistical analysis

claim: Root exudation is a well-established regulator of soil microbial decomposition and the associated release of soil carbon as carbon dioxide.
source: In turn, root exudation is a well-established regulator of soil microbial decomposition and the associated release of soil carbon as carbon dioxide (Allison et al., 2010; Melillo et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to established understanding

claim: Descriptors of plant biomass represented the most important axis of trait variation in the glasshouse experiment.
source: We found that descriptors of plant biomass represented the most important axis of trait variation (Appendix 1—figure 2) and were positively related to microbial respiration (Appendix 1—figure 2a; PC1: LR = 4.43, N = 20, p = 0.035).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 2

claim: Plant biomass was positively related to microbial respiration in the glasshouse experiment.
source: We found that descriptors of plant biomass represented the most important axis of trait variation (Appendix 1—figure 2) and were positively related to microbial respiration (Appendix 1—figure 2a; PC1: LR = 4.43, N = 20, p = 0.035).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2a

claim: Lowland plant cover was low in the field experiments (mean ± SE relative cover: 4.7% ± 0.7%).
source: However, it is unlikely that increased biomass was solely responsible for lowland plant effects in the field experiments because lowland plant cover was low (mean ± SE relative cover: 4.7% ± 0.7%).
evidence: Supported by field measurements of plant cover

claim: Lowland plants displayed relationships with the alpine soil system that were qualitatively distinct from resident alpine plants in the glasshouse experiment.
source: Furthermore, in the glasshouse experiment we found that trait variation represented by the second principal axis had opposing effects on microbial respiration between lowland and alpine treatments (Appendix 1—figure 2b; treatment × PC2: LR = 5.98, N = 20, p = 0.015). Lowland plants thus displayed relationships with the alpine soil system that were qualitatively distinct from resident alpine plants.
evidence: Inferred from statistical analysis showing treatment × PC2 interaction

claim: Lowland plants on average possessed distinct traits from alpine plants in the field experiments.
source: Publicly available trait data (Kattge et al., 2020) (plant height, leaf area, seed mass, SLA, leaf carbon, leaf nitrogen; Materials and methods) relating to all species in the field experiments revealed that lowland plants on average possessed distinct traits from alpine plants (Appendix 1—figure 3a; p = 0.025).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TRY database trait data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3a

claim: Lowland plants possessed distinct traits from alpine plants under standardized conditions in the glasshouse experiment.
source: This was also the case for measured traits of lowland versus alpine plants under standardized conditions in the glasshouse experiment (multidimensional analyses: Appendix 1—figure 3b; p = 0.001).
evidence: Supported by multidimensional analysis of measured traits shown in Appendix 1—figure 3b

claim: The magnitude of soil carbon loss caused by lowland plant presence was greater in plots where lowland plants were more abundant overall in the field experiments.
source: Coupled to this, while lowland plants were present at low abundance in the field experiments (mean ± SE relative cover: 4.7% ± 0.7%), the magnitude of soil carbon loss caused by lowland plant presence was greater in plots where lowland plants were more abundant overall (Appendix 1—figure 3e; F1,14 = 5.79, p = 0.030).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of field data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3e

claim: There was no evidence that soil carbon loss in the field was related to individual lowland species identity.
source: By contrast, we found no evidence that soil carbon loss in the field was alternatively related to individual lowland species identity (Appendix 1—figure 3c, d) or the composition of the recipient alpine plant community (Appendix 1—figure 3f, g).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 3c, d

claim: There was no evidence that soil carbon loss in the field was related to the composition of the recipient alpine plant community.
source: By contrast, we found no evidence that soil carbon loss in the field was alternatively related to individual lowland species identity (Appendix 1—figure 3c, d) or the composition of the recipient alpine plant community (Appendix 1—figure 3f, g).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 3f, g

claim: Transplantation from high to low elevation affected alpine ecosystem net carbon dioxide exchange differently between regions in the field experiments.
source: We found that transplantation from high to low elevation (i.e. warming-only) affected alpine ecosystem net carbon dioxide exchange differently between regions (Figure 5a; Supplementary file 1; p = 0.040).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a with statistical analysis

claim: In the western Alps, transplantation changed the ecosystem from a net sink to a net source of carbon dioxide.
source: In the western Alps, transplantation changed the ecosystem from a net sink to a net source of carbon dioxide, whereas in the central Alps it made the ecosystem a stronger net carbon dioxide sink.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on net ecosystem exchange

claim: In the central Alps, transplantation made the ecosystem a stronger net carbon dioxide sink.
source: In the western Alps, transplantation changed the ecosystem from a net sink to a net source of carbon dioxide, whereas in the central Alps it made the ecosystem a stronger net carbon dioxide sink.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on net ecosystem exchange

claim: Transplantation accelerated rates of both gross primary production and ecosystem respiration in the field experiments.
source: This effect occurred because although transplantation accelerated rates of both gross primary production (Figure 5b; Supplementary file 1; p < 0.001) and ecosystem respiration (Figure 5c; Supplementary file 1; p < 0.001), in the western Alps it had stronger effects on ecosystem respiration and in the central Alps stronger effects on gross primary production.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b, c with statistical analysis

claim: In the western Alps, transplantation had stronger effects on ecosystem respiration than gross primary production.
source: This effect occurred because although transplantation accelerated rates of both gross primary production (Figure 5b; Supplementary file 1; p < 0.001) and ecosystem respiration (Figure 5c; Supplementary file 1; p < 0.001), in the western Alps it had stronger effects on ecosystem respiration and in the central Alps stronger effects on gross primary production.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental data on GPP and ER

claim: In the central Alps, transplantation had stronger effects on gross primary production than ecosystem respiration.
source: This effect occurred because although transplantation accelerated rates of both gross primary production (Figure 5b; Supplementary file 1; p < 0.001) and ecosystem respiration (Figure 5c; Supplementary file 1; p < 0.001), in the western Alps it had stronger effects on ecosystem respiration and in the central Alps stronger effects on gross primary production.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental data on GPP and ER

claim: Lowland plants had no significant bearing over net ecosystem exchange in the field experiments.
source: Importantly, lowland plants had no significant bearing over net ecosystem exchange (Figure 5a), implying that although lowland plants were associated with soil carbon loss from warmed alpine plots (Figure 1), this must have occurred prior to carbon dioxide measurements being taken and was no longer actively occurring.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a

claim: Gross primary production in warmed alpine plots was unaffected by lowland plant presence in the field experiments.
source: Gross primary production in warmed alpine plots was also unaffected by lowland plant presence (Figure 5b), which is consistent with the low abundance of lowland plants in alpine communities (mean ± SE relative cover: 4.7% ± 0.7%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b

claim: Ecosystem respiration in warmed alpine plots was depressed in the presence versus absence of lowland plants in the field experiments.
source: By contrast, ecosystem respiration in warmed alpine plots was depressed in the presence versus absence of lowland plants (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c

claim: Biomass-specific rates of microbial respiration in the field were greater following transplantation to the warmer site in the presence, but not absence, of lowland plants.
source: We found that biomass-specific rates of microbial respiration in the field were greater following transplantation to the warmer site in the presence, but not absence, of lowland plants (Figure 6a; Supplementary file 1; p = 0.038).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a with statistical analysis

claim: Biomass-specific rates of microbial growth were slower following transplantation but remained unaffected by lowland plant presence in the field experiments.
source: By contrast, biomass-specific rates of microbial growth were slower following transplantation but remained unaffected by lowland plant presence (Figure 6b; Supplementary file 1; p = 0.016).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b with statistical analysis

claim: Lowland plants caused a reduction of microbial biomass carbon in alpine communities transplanted to the warmer site in the field experiments.
source: However, in the field we found that lowland plants caused a reduction of microbial biomass carbon in alpine communities transplanted to the warmer site (Figure 6c; Supplementary file 1; p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c with statistical analysis

claim: There was no change to microbial respiration per unit of soil in the presence of lowland plants in the field experiments.
source: As such, although microbes generally respired intrinsically faster in the presence of lowland plants, in the field they had become less abundant and so we observed no change to microbial respiration when expressed per unit of soil (Figure 6d; Supplementary file 1; p = 0.550).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d with statistical analysis

claim: Soil microbes are chiefly carbon limited.
source: The decline in microbial biomass likely took place because soil microbes are chiefly carbon limited (Hobbie and Hobbie, 2013), making their abundance tightly coupled to soil carbon content (here: r26 = 0.61, p = 0.001) (Walker et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hobbie and Hobbie, 2013 and correlation analysis

claim: Microbial abundance is tightly coupled to soil carbon content.
source: The decline in microbial biomass likely took place because soil microbes are chiefly carbon limited (Hobbie and Hobbie, 2013), making their abundance tightly coupled to soil carbon content (here: r26 = 0.61, p = 0.001) (Walker et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis (r26 = 0.61, p = 0.001) and citation to Walker et al., 2018

claim: A reduction in microbial biomass translated into a decline in microbial growth per unit of soil in the field experiments.
source: Moreover, since intrinsic rates of microbial growth were unaffected by lowland plant presence, a reduction in microbial biomass translated into a decline in microbial growth per unit of soil (Figure 6e; Supplementary file 1; Supplementary file 1; p = 0.009) – preventing any recovery of microbial biomass via growth (Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e with statistical analysis

claim: The decrease in soil carbon content observed in warmer transplanted plots containing lowland plants had both started and stopped within one season.
source: In short, we propose based on these relationships that the decrease in soil carbon content observed in warmer transplanted plots containing lowland plants had both started and stopped within one season.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of experimental evidence

claim: There was no evidence that soil microbes changed their resource use strategy (carbon use efficiency) in the presence versus absence of lowland plants in the field experiments.
source: We also found no evidence that soil microbes instead changed their resource use strategy in the presence versus absence of lowland plants (i.e. carbon use efficiency; Figure 6f; Supplementary file 1; p < 0.001; Tukey: p = 0.996), pointing away from microbial acclimation as an alternative mechanism.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6f with statistical analysis

claim: Uphill migrations of native lowland plants have the capacity to facilitate warming effects on soil carbon loss from alpine ecosystems.
source: In summary, we show that uphill migrations of native lowland plants have the capacity to facilitate warming effects on soil carbon loss from alpine ecosystems.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental findings

claim: Plant range expansions between herbaceous plant communities have the potential to contribute to climate feedbacks.
source: This is important because it demonstrates that plant range expansions between herbaceous plant communities have the potential to contribute to climate feedbacks.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental findings

claim: Woody species expansions in the Arctic can slow carbon turnover in herbaceous communities and yield a negative climate feedback.
source: These results contrast with expectations from woody species expansions in the Arctic, where shrubs with recalcitrant litter can slow carbon turnover in herbaceous communities and yield a negative climate feedback (Pearson et al., 2013; Cornelissen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pearson et al., 2013 and Cornelissen et al., 2007

claim: The influence of range expanding species on ecosystem carbon dynamics depends on the relative trait composition of migrating species versus the recipient community.
source: We thus suggest that the influence of range expanding species on ecosystem carbon dynamics depends on the relative trait composition of migrating species versus the recipient community (Bjorkman et al., 2018), as well as subsequent effects on environmental processes (Pearson et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and citation to Bjorkman et al., 2018

claim: Decreases in soil carbon content occurred rapidly despite a low abundance of lowland plants in the field experiments.
source: Nevertheless, here decreases in soil carbon content occurred rapidly despite a low abundance of lowland plants, and increased with total lowland plant cover.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Decreases in soil carbon content increased with total lowland plant cover in the field experiments.
source: Nevertheless, here decreases in soil carbon content occurred rapidly despite a low abundance of lowland plants, and increased with total lowland plant cover.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relationship between lowland plant cover and soil carbon loss

claim: Both warming and associated plant migrations will intensify over time.
source: Given that both warming and associated plant migrations will intensify over time (Rumpf et al., 2018; Steinbauer et al., 2018), our estimates of lowland plant impacts may be conservative – particularly if increases in lowland plant cover or repeated establishment events cause recurrent pulses of soil carbon release.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rumpf et al., 2018 and Steinbauer et al., 2018

claim: Alpine ecosystems store only a small fraction of total global soil carbon.
source: Moreover, while alpine ecosystems store only a small fraction of total global soil carbon (Streit et al., 2014; Parker et al., 2015), redistributions among herbaceous plant communities are occurring globally (Parmesan, 2006; Lenoir and Svenning, 2015; Pecl et al., 2017; Dolezal et al., 2016; Rumpf et al., 2018; Steinbauer et al., 2018), including in similarly cool ecosystems in the Arctic that contain vast soil carbon stocks (Tarnocai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Streit et al., 2014 and Parker et al., 2015

claim: Redistributions among herbaceous plant communities are occurring globally.
source: Moreover, while alpine ecosystems store only a small fraction of total global soil carbon (Streit et al., 2014; Parker et al., 2015), redistributions among herbaceous plant communities are occurring globally (Parmesan, 2006; Lenoir and Svenning, 2015; Pecl et al., 2017; Dolezal et al., 2016; Rumpf et al., 2018; Steinbauer et al., 2018), including in similarly cool ecosystems in the Arctic that contain vast soil carbon stocks (Tarnocai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting global plant redistributions

claim: Arctic ecosystems contain vast soil carbon stocks.
source: Moreover, while alpine ecosystems store only a small fraction of total global soil carbon (Streit et al., 2014; Parker et al., 2015), redistributions among herbaceous plant communities are occurring globally (Parmesan, 2006; Lenoir and Svenning, 2015; Pecl et al., 2017; Dolezal et al., 2016; Rumpf et al., 2018; Steinbauer et al., 2018), including in similarly cool ecosystems in the Arctic that contain vast soil carbon stocks (Tarnocai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tarnocai et al., 2009

claim: Elevation-based transplant experiments are powerful tools for assessing climate warming effects on ecosystems.
source: Elevation-based transplant experiments are powerful tools for assessing climate warming effects on ecosystems because they expose plots to a real-world future temperature regime with natural diurnal and seasonal cycles while also warming both above- and belowground subsystems (Hannah, 2022; Shaver et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hannah, 2022; Shaver et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2018

claim: The western Alps experiment involved warming of 2.8°C.
source: This is especially true if they include rigorous disturbance controls (here, see Materials and methods) and are performed in multiple locations where the common change from high to low elevation is temperature (here, warming of 2.8°C in the central Alps and 5.3°C in the western Alps).
evidence: Calculated from temperature differences between high and low elevation sites in Materials and methods

claim: The central Alps experiment involved warming of 5.3°C.
source: This is especially true if they include rigorous disturbance controls (here, see Materials and methods) and are performed in multiple locations where the common change from high to low elevation is temperature (here, warming of 2.8°C in the central Alps and 5.3°C in the western Alps).
evidence: Calculated from temperature differences between high and low elevation sites in Materials and methods

claim: The transplantation process had no effect on alpine soil carbon content.
source: The transplantation process had no effect on alpine soil carbon content, in that we found no difference in soil carbon content between replanted alpine control turfs at high-elevation sites and undisturbed alpine soil in the surrounding area (LR = 2.27, N = 16, p = 0.132).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of control experiment

claim: Soil from low-elevation sites contained less carbon than soil from alpine sites.
source: Nevertheless, it is well established that climate warming promotes soil carbon loss (Melillo et al., 2002; Crowther et al., 2016; Davidson and Janssens, 2006), and we found that soil from low-elevation sites (i.e. the potential end-member for warming alpine ecosystems) contained less carbon than soil from the alpine sites (70.1 ± 3.05 mg C g−1 soil dry mass compared to 145.0 ± 5.29 mg C g−1 soil dry mass; LR = 37.2, N = 27, p < 0.001), validating our expectation that alpine soil would lose carbon under warming.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with statistical analysis

claim: The alpine soil microbial community was resistant to the introduction of low-elevation soil biota.
source: We found that the alpine soil microbial community was resistant to the introduction of low-elevation soil biota, in that inoculation had no effect on soil bacterial (Appendix 1—figure 4a; PERMANOVA; F1,9 = 0.75, p = 0.573) or fungal (Appendix 1—figure 4b; F1,9 = 0.75, p = 0.774) community composition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4 with statistical analysis

claim: Transplantation to the warmer site increased alpine soil bulk density in the central Alps experiment.
source: We found that although transplantation to the warmer site increased alpine soil bulk density (LR = 7.18, p = 0.028, Tukey: p < 0.05), lowland plants had no effect (Tukey: p = 0.999).
evidence: Supported by measurements taken in 2021 with statistical analysis

claim: Lowland plants had no effect on soil bulk density in the central Alps experiment.
